problem_markdown: In acute triangle $ABC$, the internal angle bisectors meet its circumcircle again at $A_1,B_1,C_1$. Let $A_0,B_0,C_0$ be the corresponding excenters. Prove $[A_0B_0C_0]=2[AC_1BA_1CB_1]\ge4[ABC]$.
solutions_markdown:
Let $I$ be the incenter. The arc-midpoint lemma gives $A_1B=A_1C=A_1I=A_1A_0$; in particular $A_1$ is the midpoint of $IA_0$. One proof uses $\angle IBA_0=\angle ICA_0=90^\circ$, placing $B,C$ on the circle with diameter $IA_0$, whose centre lies on $AA_0$ and on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, hence at $A_1$ when the two lines are distinct. In the isosceles case the same midpoint identity follows by continuity from non-isosceles triangles.

Therefore $[IBA_0C]=2[IBA_1C]$, and the two cyclic versions also hold. Summing these three area decompositions of the excentral triangle and the hexagon proves the identity.

Let $H$ be the orthocenter, which lies inside $ABC$. Its reflection across $BC$ lies on the circumcircle on the arc $BC$ away from $A$. The arc midpoint $A_1$ maximises the perpendicular distance to $BC$ on that arc. Hence $[BCH]\le[BCA_1]$. Summing the three versions gives
$$[ABC]\le[BCA_1]+[CAB_1]+[ABC_1].$$
The hexagon is the original triangle plus these three exterior caps, so its area is at least $2[ABC]$. The claimed second inequality follows from the identity.
